item.title: Status 2.39: Reliable message delivery, new token Swap+ Bridge, browser Incognito mode, Robinhood chain, and more…
item.description:
Status 2.39 brings a wide range of new features and improvements across messaging, wallet, browser, communities, Keycard, performance, navigation, and p2p network status visibility.

One of the major additions is the full rollout of SDS (Scalable Data Sync) protocol in Status Communities, bringing  reliable message delivery and confirmation,
item.dc:creator: Bobby Zalke
item.content:encoded:
Status 2.39 brings a wide range of new features and improvements across messaging, wallet, browser, communities, Keycard, performance, navigation, and p2p network status visibility.

One of the major additions is the full rollout of SDS (Scalable Data Sync) protocol in Status Communities, bringing  reliable message delivery and confirmation, while the app automatically ensures no messages are missed. But there is a lot more in this release.

Important: This is a breaking change. If you’re on Status v2.36.1 or lower, you must update to v2.39. Otherwise, your Status app won’t be able to properly communicate with Status users on v2.39.

Update to v2.39

Release Highlights

  1. Reliable message delivery and confirmation for communities
  2. Cross-chain + cross-account token swaps and bridges in one go
  3. Mobile browser got Incognito mode and file downloads & opening
  4. Meet Status team bot
  5. Robinhood chain support
  6. French, Czech & Ukrainian translations
  7. New Keycard user experience
  8. Writing & editing messages got easier
  9. Adjustable interface zoom
  10. Easier back navigation across the app
  11. Better feedback when fetching a community
  12. More responsive mobile experience
  13. Visibility into P2P network connection
  14. See your unread notifications from the taskbar
  15. Easier copy, cut, and paste in input fields
  16. Flatpak support
  17. Zoom in on images in chats
  18. Private, decentralized community history with Logos Storage 

Messaging and Communities

Reliable message delivery for communities with full SDS protocol rollout

Status 2.39 marks the full rollout of the SDS (Scalable Data Sync) protocol, bringing reliable message delivery to Status communities. Starting with this release, the app can receive, understand, and send SDS messages.

With the SDS protocol now fully activated in Status communities, you can see whether your messages have been delivered (the “Delivered” double tick next to your sent messages), while the app automatically ensures no messages are missed.

Learn more about SDS (Scalable Data Sync), how the protocol works, and what it means for Status communities in the full article: Status Communities Get Reliable Messaging with the SDS Protocol.

Update to v2.39

Meet Status Team peer-to-peer bot

Now, Status has an official Status Team peer-to-peer bot for updates, how-to tips, contacting the team, sharing feedback, reporting issues, or suggesting features. It speaks English only for now, with more languages coming. If you’re a new user, the bot will welcome you and send how-to tips to help you set up Status and explore its features.

The bot is a peer-to-peer contact on the decentralised network. To chat with it, send a contact request just as you would to any other Status contact (look for the Status icon above your profile picture in the main navigation bar). Messages use the same end-to-end encrypted, peer-to-peer messaging as your other Status chats. You can disconnect from the bot at any time.

The bot will occasionally send Status updates and how-to tips, and gives you an easy and quick way to share feedback, contact the team, report issues, or suggest features.

Importantly, the Status Team bot never contacts you first.
Update your Status to connect with the Status Team bot

Writing, editing, and replying to messages just got easier

Status 2.39 delivers the second phase of the revamped chat input field, with several improvements designed to make composing and interacting with messages easier. Text formatting, tagging users, pasting links over text, quoting, editing, and replying now feel more intuitive and seamless.

Writing messages, made easier

Writing messages has been revamped to make the user writing experience more efficient and productive while composing a message. Formatting text, mentioning someone, adding links over text, and quoting content is now more intuitive and seamless.

A mobile-friendly context menu

This release also introduces a mobile-friendly context menu in the chat. A simple long press gives you quick access to your most recent emojis and most-used chat actions without needing to navigate through the full context menu.

Editing messages is easier

The message editing experience has been improved as well. Updating something you have already sent is now more straightforward, making it easier to quickly correct or change a message.

Try the new chat tools now! 

Share contacts directly in direct messages

You can now easily share contacts in direct messages. Type @, or select @ from the chat input quick action bar, and choose the contact you want to share.

A better reply-to-message experience

The reply experience has also been improved. Replying to messages now feels more intuitive and responsive, making it easier to follow and continue conversations.

Better feedback when fetching a community for the first time

Opening a community link for the first time requires Status to fetch the community before it can be displayed. Status 2.39 now makes this process clearer.

When you open a community invite or channel link for the first time, Status shows a loading screen while fetching the Community. If the community cannot be fetched within 60 seconds, you are given the option to retry or cancel.

This gives you clearer feedback instead of leaving you unsure whether anything is happening while Status fetches a community for the first time.

Get Status to start or join  a Community

Privacy, Browser and P2P Network

Mobile Web Browser now has Incognito mode, file downloads and opening, and  data cleanup

The Status Mobile Web Browser gets several new features in 2.39, including Incognito mode, file downloads and opening, and  ways to clear browsing data.

Browse with Incognito mode

Status Mobile Browser now has an Incognito mode for more private browsing, helping you leave less of a digital footprint on your device by not keeping your browsing history, cookies, or site data after the session ends.

Clear site and browsing data

Sometimes a web page may not work or load properly, so now you have two ways to reset it:

  • Clear site data lets you reset the data associated with your currently active web page.
  • Clear browsing data clears cache and cookies across the entire browser.

This makes it easier to fix website rendering issues and manage your browsing data . 

Download and open files from the browser

You can now download and open various files directly through the Status Mobile Web Browser. There is also a new Supported formats feature in the browser menu. This shows which file formats the browser can open based on your platform’s browser engine.

Ready to browse?  Give it a try.

New visibility into your P2P network connection

Since Status messaging works through a peer-to-peer network, your connection to that network is an important part of the experience. Status now makes it easier to know whether you’re connected to the peer-to-peer network.

If Status loses its P2P connection, you will now see a banner letting you know. The banner also provides guidance on what to check to get connected again. You can also go to:

Settings → P2P network

at any time to see your current P2P connectivity status and the number of connected network peers.

Wallet and Keycard

Cross-chain & cross-account token Swap + Bridge in one go 

Here we go… This is happening. Status now has a fast and simple way to swap and bridge across chains and wallet accounts, with a completely revamped user experience.

Now, you don’t have to choose between swapping or bridging upfront. You can do both in a single go via one unified Swap & Bridge interface to move your tokens across chains and accounts.

The new Swap & Bridge interface enables swapping and bridging tokens to your wallet accounts or directly to other addresses outside your wallet in a single go, without having to go through a sequence of intermediary steps to move your tokens across different chains and addresses.

It works across all the blockchain networks supported by Status, with routes provided by Relay to find the best available quote.

Simply choose your sending account and token on a particular network, then any receiving account and token on the network of your choice, drag the slider to set the percentage of the token you want to send, review the quote and route, and confirm. You can even swap a token on one network and receive a different token in another account on another network  all in one go, without manually swapping, bridging, and transferring assets through multiple transactions.

Try Swap & Bridge

New Keycard user experience

Status 2.39 introduces a completely redesigned Keycard experience focused on reducing unnecessary interactions and making user flows simpler and intuitive. On Mobile, the team has revamped Keycard support so that device–Keycard interactions can now be completed with a single tap.

Whether you’re:

  • setting up Keycard
  • logging in
  • signing transactions

you no longer need to tap your Keycard multiple times during the same flow. Now the Keycard user flows are  way simpler, better structured, and more efficient.

Robinhood Chain is now available in Status

Status 2.39 adds support for the Robinhood Chain. You can now use Status to view balances, send and receive tokens and NFTs, swap and bridge, and interact with dApps on Robinhood Chain. 

Everything you need to use Robinhood Chain is now available directly in Status 

Explore Robinhood Chain in Status

Smoother User Experience

Status now speaks French, Czech, and Ukrainian

Status is now available in French, Czech, and Ukrainian.

As Status grows globally, making the app accessible in more languages becomes increasingly important. Whether you are in France, Czechia, Ukraine, or elsewhere across the French-, Czech-, and Ukrainian-speaking world, you can now use Status in your preferred language.

More languages are on the way.

Switch to your preferred language now! 

Smoother and more responsive mobile experience

Status 2.39 also includes a number of improvements across the mobile app focused on making everyday interactions smoother and more responsive across a wider range of devices.

These improvements are particularly noticeable on less powerful phones, including some devices with 4 GB of RAM, as well as Samsung foldable phones.

The changes include:

  • snappier navigation
  • shorter login times
  • faster password changes
  • improvements to loading and displaying data across the app
  • dialogs that better adapt to different screen sizes and orientations

Performance improvement work will continue in Status v2.40 and v2.41. These releases will bring more substantial performance improvements, especially for less powerful mobile devices  :

  • faster opening and loading of pages and tabs
  • lower CPU usage
  • lower RAM usage
  • reduced battery consumption

More responsive buttons and interactions

Buttons, icons, dropdowns, and list options now visually respond when you tap or click them. This makes interactions feel more immediate and gives you clearer feedback that your action was recognized.

Clearer message sending and retry experience

The message sending experience has also been improved across Status. Messages that are currently being sent now appear normally instead of looking faded. If a message fails to send, the failed state and Resend action are easier to see and access.

This makes it clearer when a message needs your attention. More improvements to the message sending experience are planned for v2.40.

Update Status on your phone

Set Status to your preferred size with Interface Zoom

You can now adjust Interface Zoom in Status.

Interface Zoom scales both the app interface and text, letting you choose a size that feels more comfortable on your screen.

By default, Status automatically follows your device’s system zoom setting, but you can manually adjust the zoom level to suit your preferences.

Easier back navigation across the app

Going back through Status now works more like you would expect from the rest of your device. On Android, you can use the system Back button. On Desktop, you can use your mouse Back button or keyboard shortcut.

These controls let you quickly navigate back through screens you previously opened.

Zoom in on images in chats

Images shared in Status chats can now be zoomed in to take a closer look at details. On Mobile, use pinch-to-zoom. On Desktop, use Ctrl + mouse wheel to zoom in and out of an opened image.  

See unread notifications from the taskbar

On Desktop, the Status app icon in the taskbar can now show a badge with your unread notification count, so you can see when there’s something new in Status without opening the app.

 The unread count respects the notification preferences you have configured under:

Settings → Notifications

Easier copy, cut, and paste across input fields

Copying, cutting, and pasting text is now easier in all input fields across platforms.

Use:

  • Tap on iOS
  • Long press on Android
  • Right click on Desktop

to open the text editing context menu and quickly copy, cut, or paste text.

Status is now available as a Flatpak

Linux users now have another way to install Status.

Status is available as a Flatpak, providing an easier and more consistent way to install and update Status across different Linux distributions.

Install Status as a Flatpak

Privacy-preserving, decentralized Community history with Logos Storage

Status now supports Logos Storage protocol for storing and retrieving Community message history. Community history archives can be shared and replicated across a decentralized peer-to-peer network of participating nodes, making historical messages available to Community members.

Compared with the existing BitTorrent-based Archive Protocol, Logos Storage protocol is designed with privacy-preserving file sharing as a core goal.

For most users, this happens behind the scenes. When historical Community messages are needed, Status can retrieve the relevant archives from participating peers and make those messages available in the Community.

Want to try it? Go to Settings  on Status Desktop → Advanced → Archive Protocol → Logos Storage. You can switch back to Torrent or disable the Archive Protocol from the same setting.

Update now

Note

Status is under active development, so you may occasionally encounter bugs or unexpected behaviour. .

Your feedback helps us build the best app for secure crypto, private messaging, and community-owned spaces. Read this guide for more information on reporting bugs in Status. Alternatively, you can share your feedback directly in the Desktop or Mobile feedback channels within the Status Community.

Don’t miss the latest news from Status – follow us on X or join our Community in the Status app to get the latest news and updates!

Your use of the Status apps is subject to the Status Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

item.title: When Your Recovery Phrase Isn’t Random Enough
item.description:
More than $100M worth of Bitcoin has been linked to thefts involving a weakness in COLDCARD seed generation.

The surprising part: attackers did not need to steal the hardware wallet, connect to it, or know the PIN.

The problem started when some wallets created their recovery phrase.

COLDCARD disclosed
item.dc:creator: Bobby Zalke
item.content:encoded:
More than $100M worth of Bitcoin has been linked to thefts involving a weakness in COLDCARD seed generation.

The surprising part: attackers did not need to steal the hardware wallet, connect to it, or know the PIN.

The problem started when some wallets created their recovery phrase.

COLDCARD disclosed that affected firmware did not always get randomness from the hardware random-number generator as intended. In some cases, recovery phrase generation could fall back to a much more predictable software path. For affected Mk2/Mk3 devices, Coinkite estimates the effective entropy could fall to roughly 40 bits.

For context, a normal 12-word BIP-39 recovery phrase starts from 128 bits of entropy. The BIP-39 standard allows 128–256 bits.

That difference matters a lot.

First: what does “randomness” actually mean?

When a wallet gives you 12 words of your wallet recovery phrase like:

word → word → word → word…

it is not simply choosing words randomly from a list, behind those words is a much larger random number.

That randomness is called entropy.

The wallet uses that entropy to create your recovery phrase, which is then used to derive your wallet keys. If the original randomness is strong and unpredictable, guessing the recovery phrase is practically impossible.

But if the randomness becomes predictable, an attacker does not need to search every possible 12-word phrase. They only need to search through the much smaller group of phrases the faulty generator could have produced.

That is what made the COLDCARD issue so serious.

Is using your device for randomness unusual?

No.

Using a phone or computer's cryptographically secure random-number generator, or CSPRNG, is a normal building block in modern security software. Apple provides system randomization APIs specifically for generating cryptographically secure random bytes.

The widely used BitcoinJS libraries also rely on cryptographic randomness provided by the environment. Its BIP-39 implementation uses crypto.randomBytes underneath and defaults to 128 bits of entropy when generating a recovery phrase.

BitcoinJS also documents that its broader library uses browser window.crypto.getRandomValues or Node's crypto.randomBytes for random-number generation.

Trust Wallet's open-source Wallet Core similarly describes BIP-39 recovery phrase creation beginning with 128–256 bits of entropy, with 128 bits producing a 12-word recovery phrase. So the basic idea is widely established:

Use a cryptographically secure source of entropy → feed that entropy into the wallet's key/seed-generation process.

The important part is not whether the randomness comes from “software” or “hardware” by itself.

The important part is whether that source is cryptographically secure, unpredictable, correctly implemented and falls back safely.

So what does Status do?

Status does not generate recovery phrases the same way COLDCARD did. 

When Status creates a new recovery phrase, the randomness comes from the phone or computer's operating-system secure random generator. Status uses Go's crypto/rand, which is backed by the operating system's cryptographically secure random source.

For the standard 12-word Status recovery phrase, the process starts from 128 bits of entropy and strictly follows BIP-39 mnemonic generation.

In simple terms:

Your device generates secure random bytes→ those bytes become entropy→ BIP-39 turns that entropy into your 12-word recovery phrase.

The important difference from the COLDCARD incident is that Status does not implement the same hardware-RNG/software-fallback mechanism that led to that specific vulnerability; it relies on the operating system's cryptographically secure random-number generator instead.

What about Status + Keycard?

 When you create your Status profile with Keycard, the recovery phrase is generated by Status on your phone or computer, using the operating system's cryptographically secure randomness, and is then loaded onto the card. Keycard then adds another security layer by protecting how your keys are stored and used.

 Status recovery phrase generation creates the recovery phrase using cryptographically secure operating system's randomness and writes it on Keycard.

Keycard holds the private keys and performs signing inside the card, so the keys are not handed back to the phone or computer for everyday use. 

There is one more important detail

If someone generated a recovery phrase using an affected COLDCARD version and later imported that same recovery phrase into a different wallet, the original weakness would still remain.

That is because the weakness belongs to the recovery phrase itself, not the wallet app it is later imported into.

Moving a weak recovery phrase to another wallet does not add new entropy or make it stronger. The safer approach is to generate an entirely new recovery phrase from a secure source and move the assets to the new wallet.

The bigger lesson

A hardware wallet can be offline.Your recovery phrase can be written on paper.Your keys can never touch a cloud server.

But all of that security still depends on one very early step: Was the recovery phrase created with enough unpredictable randomness in the first place?

Recovery phrase security starts before storage.It starts with entropy.

item.title: Elements of Private, Secure Messaging Apps
item.description:
Privacy in messaging is often reduced to a single feature: encryption.

But private communication is not defined by one mechanism. It is the result of multiple layers working together each addressing a different type of privacy risk.

Over time, both user expectations and system architectures have evolved. Messaging apps today
item.dc:creator: Bobby Zalke
item.content:encoded:
Privacy in messaging is often reduced to a single feature: encryption.

But private communication is not defined by one mechanism. It is the result of multiple layers working together each addressing a different type of privacy risk.

Over time, both user expectations and system architectures have evolved. Messaging apps today are no longer just communication tools, but they are platforms that interact with identity, data, and networks at scale.

This makes it important to revisit what “private messaging” actually means in practice.

1. End-to-End Encryption (E2EE)

End-to-end encryption ensures that only the sender and the intended recipient can read the content of a message. Messages are encrypted on the sender’s device and decrypted only on the recipient’s device.

This protects against:

  • unauthorized reading of messages even if they are intercepted during transmission,
  • message content being accessed by servers, network providers, or other intermediaries.

Apps like WhatsApp and Signal implement E2EE by default for messages and calls.

Telegram offers E2EE only in “Secret chats,” not in standard conversations.

Discord does not provide end-to-end encryption for regular messages.

Even though end-to-end encryption protects message content, it does not extend to metadata such as participant identities, timing, or interaction patterns.

Recent cases have shown that attackers often bypass encryption entirely through:

social engineering
account takeover (verification code phishing)
spyware at the device level

These do not break E2EE itself, but show that secure messaging depends on more than just encryption alone.

That is why Status starts with end-to-end encryption, but does not stop there. Status uses end-to-end encryption for direct, group, and community messages and complements it with anonymous account creation, cryptographic identity, decentralized peer-to-peer messaging network, and a privacy-first design that minimizes metadata exposure.

The point is not only to protect what you communicate. The point is to reduce how much the system can infer about your conversation.

2. Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) & Post-Compromise Security (PCS)

Perfect forward secrecy is designed to protect your past messages even if the encryption keys used for your current session are later compromised. End-to-end encryption ensures only the intended participants can read messages in the first place while PFS adds a second layer, so that a single key compromise doesn't unravel your entire message history.

In simple terms: if one key is exposed, it should not unlock messages you sent before that point.

Separately, secure messengers also aim for post-compromise security: the ability for a session to "heal" itself after a compromise, so an attacker who briefly gains access still loses the ability to read future messages once new key material is exchanged. Together, perfect forward secrecy and post-compromise security are what the Signal Protocol's Double Ratchet, which is used by apps like WhatsApp and Signal, is built to provide.

Recent security research shows why forward secrecy must be part of a wider system, but not just treated as a standalone guarantee.

In 2025, researchers demonstrated a targeted prekey depletion attack against WhatsApp's handshake mechanism, showing that under specific conditions it could degrade some of the protocol's intended security properties, including perfect forward secrecy for certain messages. Separately, WhatsApp patched a vulnerability (CVE-2025-55177) that Meta said may have been exploited alongside an Apple OS vulnerability (CVE-2025-43300) in sophisticated targeted attacks.

This does not mean encryption is useless. It means attackers usually don't need to "break encryption" directly. They target edge cases, implementation details, devices, recovery flows, or the surrounding infrastructure instead.

Status uses the Double Ratchet algorithm, where conversation keys keep evolving over time, so a single compromised key shouldn't unlock the full message history or grant the ability to read future messages once new key material is exchanged. Perfect forward secrecy protects the past while Post-compromise security protects the future. Status pairs both with cryptographic identity and a decentralized peer-to-peer message network to extend protection beyond just message content.

3. Anonymous Account Creation

Most messaging apps require some form of third party validation when creating an account - often a phone number, but sometimes an email address. Some platforms also tie accounts to payment methods or social services.

  • WhatsApp → phone number required
  • Telegram → phone number required
  • Signal → requires a phone number for account creation, but is adding support for usernames to allow users to communicate without sharing their phone number.

This is where the comparison becomes important.

  • Signal protects message content, but still begins with a phone number.
  • Telegram lets users hide phone numbers in some contexts, but still requires one at signup.
  • WhatsApp encrypts personal messages, but its identity layer is built around phone numbers.
  • Discord is flexible for communities, but not built around private cryptographic identities and encrypted messaging.

While on Status, you do not need a phone number, email address, or social login to create a Status profile. Your identity is generated from cryptographic keys on your own device.

That means Status does not begin private communication by asking users to attach themselves to a telecom identifier. This is a major difference. Other apps often add privacy controls after identity has already been linked. Status starts from anonymous identity first.

4. Network Architecture

The way messages move across a network determines how much control and visibility exists.

Most mainstream apps rely on centralized infrastructure:

  • WhatsApp
  • Telegram
  • Discord

In these systems:

  • messages are routed through company-controlled servers
  • operators control delivery, storage, and policy enforcement

This creates:

  • single points of failure
  • centralized surveillance
  • dependency on platform policies

Incidents like these show that risks in centralized platforms often extend beyond the core messaging layer.

That is the real lesson: privacy risk often lives around the messenger, not only inside the chat window.

Status messaging is powered by Logos Messaging network (Formerly known as Waku), a decentralized peer-to-peer communication protocol designed for privacy-focused and censorship-resistant messaging. Instead of routing every message through central company-controlled servers, Status messages move through a decentralized network. Store nodes used to temporarily hold encrypted messages for offline users only operate with encrypted messages and have no knowledge or possession of any decryption keys.

Status does not require users to trust a single central operator with the entire communication system. By separating identity, message content, and message transport, it reduces the amount of information any single party can observe about your communications.

5. Metadata Exposure

Even when messages are encrypted, metadata is still generated and processed. Metadata describes the context of communication rather than its content.

This includes:

  • who communicates with whom
  • when messages are sent and received
  • frequency of interaction
  • device and network signals

For example:

  • WhatsApp collects usage and interaction data
  • Telegram processes activity within its cloud-based system
  • Discord retains and processes user interaction data

Unlike message content, metadata is often harder for users to observe or control, yet it can still provide significant insight into user behaviour.

Status is designed to reduce metadata exposure at multiple layers, including disabling any third-party providers used in Status to turn it into a completely sandboxed environment right from the moment users onboard.

By using cryptographic identities instead of phone numbers and routing messages through a decentralized peer-to-peer network, Status is designed to reduce the amount of linkable data created by default.

6. Account Recovery Can Become an Attack Surface

Most people think about messaging security in terms of hackers breaking encryption.

In reality, many attacks target the softer layers: account recovery, customer support, device compromise, social engineering, and authentication workflows.

This has become even more important as platforms add AI agents into support and account-management flows.

Recently, hackers tricked Meta’s AI support chatbot into helping them take over Instagram accounts by linking attacker-controlled email addresses to target accounts and triggering password resets. High-profile accounts were reportedly affected, including the Obama-era White House Instagram account and Sephora. Meta said the issue was fixed.

This was not a classic encryption failure.

It was an authority failure.

A support system was given too much power over identity and recovery. Once that layer failed, the account could be taken over without breaking the cryptography of any private message.

This is why identity design matters.

When accounts are tied to phone numbers, emails, centralized support systems, or platform-controlled recovery flows, the messenger inherits those attack surfaces.

Status avoids this by making cryptographic keys central to identity. Your profile is not created through a phone number or email address, and the architecture is designed around user-controlled keys rather than a centralized identity provider.

That does not remove every risk. Users still need to secure their devices and backups.

But it does remove an entire class of platform-controlled identity dependencies.

Conclusion

With surveillance on the rise and massive financial incentives for organizations of all types to extract personal data, finding means of preserving our privacy is crucial. Choosing a private, secure messenger is one way to do so.

Status is designed around the idea that privacy is not a single feature, but a combination of decisions across identity, network, and data handling.

Status combines multiple layers of privacy into a single architecture:

Messages are end-to-end encrypted using the double ratchet algorithm, meaning only intended participants can read them and keys keep evolving, so even if one is compromised, past and future messages remain secure.

Instead of using phone numbers or emails, identity is created from cryptographic keypairs generated on your device. This allows you to interact anonymously by default, without exposing real-world identifiers unless you choose to.

At the network level, Status messaging is powered by Logos Messaging network (formally known as WAKU), a decentralized peer-to-peer messaging protocol. Messages aren’t sent through central company-controlled servers; they’re broadcast across a network of peer-to-peer nodes and picked up by the recipient. Store nodes used to temporarily hold encrypted messages for offline users only operate with encrypted messages and have no knowledge or possession of any decryption keys.

By separating identity, message content, and message transport, Status reduces the amount of information any single party can observe about your communications.

That’s the key difference: privacy isn’t added on top. It’s built into how Status works end to end.
